units: prolonged stillness in a seated position loads the spine
the deep back muscles stiffen for want of movement
the pain is intermittent at first and later lasting
carers see this trouble appearing in ever younger adults

the cause lies in a slumped back rather than an injury
straightening up and moving often releases muscular tension
adjusting the seat height keeps the thighs parallel with the floor
the discomfort fades within a season in those who follow these measures
text: Sitting still for hours loads the spine far more heavily than most people suspect. Starved of movement, the deep muscles along the back gradually harden and tug at the lower vertebrae. A dull ache sets in, coming and going at first, then settling for good. Carers report the complaint in adults who are younger and younger, including plenty who have never lifted anything heavy in their lives. The cause is rarely an injury. It lies in a slumped back, shoulders rolled forward, pelvis tipped backwards. Putting that right costs almost nothing. Straightening up, walking about, stretching the muscles down the back of the legs already loosens what has built up. Raising or lowering the seat so the thighs stay parallel with the floor finishes the job. Those who keep to this see the discomfort fade within a season.

units: the main character breaks her ankle a second time as an adult
in childhood she had worn a splint without suffering morally
as a child she went on running and laughed at her uneven walk
the adult fall happens on a slippery step
as an adult she finds her walking aid heavy and trips about the house exhausting
she understands that inaction wears her out more than activity
what made her laugh as a child mortifies her as an adult
a fine mark stays on her skin once the bone has knitted
she takes up walking again by controlling every step
text: The second break was nothing like the first, and that was what caught her off guard. As a girl she had worn a light splint for a whole season without losing an ounce of her spirit; she half-ran, she hopped along corridors, she laughed at her lopsided walk. As a grown woman the same joint gave way on a wet step, and the whole business took on another colour altogether. The crutch felt heavy, the stairs hostile, the walk through to the kitchen endless. Idleness, she found, wears a body out faster than effort ever did. What had once amused her now shamed her, not out of vanity, but because she could measure what she had stopped taking for granted. When the bone knitted, a thin scar marked the skin, a quiet keepsake of an ordinary fall. She learned to walk again, watching where every step landed.

units: the first aid kit divides into three compartments
the first compartment brings together the material that covers a wound
the dressings must be sterile and wrapped separately
the second compartment gathers the products spread onto the skin

a gel treats the bites that bring on an itch
the third compartment holds what immobilises or supports a limb
the expiry dates must be checked at every change of season
the container must be rigid and kept away from heat
text: A first aid kit worth its name falls into three clearly separate compartments. The first holds whatever is needed to cover a wound: sterile dressings sealed in individual wrappers, sticking plasters in a range of widths, a roll of fixing tape and a pair of round-tipped scissors. The second gathers everything that goes onto the skin itself: an alcohol-free antiseptic solution, a soothing ointment for the lighter burns, a gel for the bites that bring on an itch. The third carries the supporting kit: an elastic bandage, a sling for the arm, a soft splint to hold a finger or a wrist still. Check the expiry dates at every change of season and replace whatever has already been opened, without hesitating. Keep the lot in a rigid box, away from any heat and out of reach of children, then write on the lid whatever has run short.

a workshop on holding the back and preventing falls came next

local representatives judge the capacity insufficient and ask for an extension
text: The news broke as the mild season opened: a rehabilitation centre was to be set up in a working-class district that had never had anything of the kind. Work began without delay inside a disused warehouse whose metal frame was kept exactly as it stood. By autumn the first rooms were taking in patients discharged after major surgery, many of them leaning on a crutch or held together by a splint. The winter that followed brought a heated pool into service, which made it possible to treat joints too painful to bear any weight on the ground. Management then announced a workshop given over to posture and to the prevention of falls, open to the older people of the area. Local representatives now hold that demand outstrips the capacity planned, and are pressing for the building to be extended.

units: the heel reddens and grows slightly warm at first
rubbing against the shoe separates the surface layers of the skin

the tension of the pouch changes the way of walking
shifting the weight onto the other foot brings on an ache in the hip

a greasy ointment spread on before walking reduces the rubbing
a final thickening of the skin makes the discomfort disappear
text: The heel turns faintly red to begin with, barely warmer than the skin lying around it. Rubbing against the shoe lifts the topmost layers apart, and a clear fluid seeps into the space that has opened up: the blister has formed. Its stretched roof makes standing on the foot painful and alters the gait, which throws the load onto the other leg and brings on, a little later, a dull ache in the hip. Should the pouch burst, the raw patch underneath turns tender and lies wide open to infection. That is why the place is covered over with a clean dressing rather than opened on purpose. A greasy ointment rubbed well in before a long walk cuts down the friction at the outset. Once the skin finally thickens over that spot, it holds up better and the soreness clears of its own accord.

units: the writer states that lack of sleep is treated as ordinary
drowsiness and short temper are put down to the load of work
sleep deprivation is never held responsible
evening screens push back the hour of going to bed
the stimulating drink the next day delays the following drop into sleep
the writer advises cutting the screens before going into the bedroom
the bedroom must be kept cool and dark
he recommends a steady bedtime, weekend included
the effects are felt after a handful of nights
sleep is presented as a repair that is owed and not as a privilege
text: Let us be honest: we sleep badly, and we have grown far too comfortable with it. The yawn that cuts across a meeting, the eyelids sagging halfway through the afternoon, the temper that sours over nothing, all of it gets blamed on the load of work, never on the nights we keep cutting short. Come evening, the screen wins: one clip, then another, and bed comes long after the hour we set ourselves. The morning after, we make up for it with coffee, which pushes the next drop into sleep later still. Getting out of that spiral is no mystery. Switch the screens off before going through to the bedroom, keep the room cool and dark, turn in at the same hour even at the weekend. It sounds bleak, yet the difference shows after a handful of nights. Sleep is no treat we grant ourselves; it is a repair we owe.

units: the physiotherapist receives her patients on her feet, with no desk between them

she now practises with elderly patients in a residential district

she works on standing stability in order to avoid falls
she says she likes this slower rhythm
her patients are looking for a confidence built up session after session
text: She greets her patients on her feet, at the door of her practice, with no desk standing between them. The physiotherapist began her career on a hospital ward given over mostly to injured sportspeople: sprains, torn muscles, the stubborn cramp that follows a badly prepared effort. The pace was quick there, the sessions short, the outcome easy to measure. She now works in a quiet residential district with elderly patients, and the job has changed in kind. Her aim is no longer to bring a knee back to top-level sport, but to teach someone to get up unaided, to climb stairs without dread, to hold a standing posture steady enough to keep them from falling. She says she prefers this slower rhythm. Where the athlete wanted a deadline, her patients want confidence, and confidence is built session after session.

units: the reviewer praises three aspects of the work and disputes only one

the reviewer finds these drawings warmer than medical photographs
the passage on aching muscles is dealt with too briefly
the reader closes the book pleased but a little disappointed
text: This handbook of home care earns praise on three counts and a reservation on one. Its first strength is the clarity of the actions it sets out: laying on a dressing, changing a pad, spotting a wound that has turned septic. Each operation is taken apart into its simplest movements, with no needless jargon. Its second virtue is restraint. The author never tires of marking the limits of care given at home, and the moment when a doctor's opinion becomes compulsory. Its third success is a matter of looks: the hand-drawn plates lend the volume a warmth that clinical photography never reaches. Then comes the reservation. The chapter on aching muscles disposes of stiffness and cramp in a single page, as though complaints that common deserved no proper study. One closes the book pleased, and a little let down.

text: I am writing to tell you how the operation turned out, since it was you who asked for the details. It was done at the end of last week under a local anaesthetic; the surgeon took out the fragment of bone that had been jamming up the joint. The following day a nurse changed the dressing and fitted a rigid splint, which I have to keep on right up until my check-up. Over the week that came after, the pain gave way, though an itch came up around the stitches, the usual sign of healing, so the care team tell me. They have put me on a neutral ointment, to be spread on without rubbing. Since the day before yesterday I have been putting the foot to the ground with a single crutch, and I take the stairs leading with the sound leg. Rehabilitation starts as soon as the stitches come out.

units: the night contraction hits a muscle already worked during the evening
a shortage of water and mineral salts locks the muscle fibres
the episode is harmless in most cases
the attack fades in very little time
stretching the muscle by drawing the toes back stops the signal
a warm compress laid on afterwards relaxes the fibre
this heat limits the muscle soreness of the next day
drinking enough in the evening and avoiding late effort prevent a return
certain medicines that make the body shed water must be watched
frequent attacks that break up sleep justify seeking advice
text: What sets off a cramp in the night? The muscle seizes when, already worked hard through the evening, it runs short of water and mineral salts; the fibres lock and refuse to let go. Is it a sign of illness? In most cases, no: the cause stays humdrum and the episode fades within moments. What should be done during the attack? Stretching the affected muscle gently, drawing the toes back towards you, breaks the signal that keeps the contraction going. A warm compress laid on afterwards eases the fibre and takes the edge off the soreness felt the next day. Can it be kept from coming back? Drink enough in the evening, avoid hard effort late on, and keep an eye on medicines that make the body shed water. When is advice needed? If attacks cut through sleep night after night, an examination is called for.
